library(countdown)

library(rsample)

library(fontawesome)

library(gt)
library(gtsummary)
library(carData)

notes_theme = theme_minimal(base_size = 12, base_family = "Source Sans 3")
theme_set(notes_theme)

regression_panel <- function(formula, scat.formula = NULL, data, xlab, ylab) {
  mod <- lm(formula, data = data)
  
  aug <- augment(mod)
  
  plot_fit <- makeFun(mod)
  
  if(is.null(scat.formula)) {
    orig_data <- gf_point(formula, data = data, xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, color = "#003300")
  } else {
    orig_data <- gf_point(scat.formula, data = data, xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, color = "#003300") 
  }
  
  orig_data <- orig_data %>% gf_fun(plot_fit(x) ~ x, color = "#f15a31")
  
  resid_plot <- gf_point(.std.resid ~ .fitted, data = aug, xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Standardized residuals") %>%
    gf_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, color = "#f15a31")
  
  qq_plot <- gf_qq(~.std.resid, data = aug, xlab = "N(0,1) quantiles", ylab = "Standardized residuals", color = "#003300") %>%
    gf_qqline(color = "#f15a31")
  
  (orig_data | resid_plot | qq_plot)
}


bikes_mlr <- lm(rides ~ temp_actual*weekend, data = bikes)

## Review: SST/SSReg/SSE

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# 1. Setup Data and Model
set.seed(42)
n <- 15
x <- seq(1, 10, length.out = n)
y <- 2 + 0.8 * x + rnorm(n, sd = 1.5)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

# Fit model and get predictions/mean
fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = df)
df$y_hat <- predict(fit)
df$y_mean <- mean(df$y)

# 2. Plot SST: Variation from the Mean (Total)
# Formula: sum((y - y_mean)^2)
p_sst <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = y_mean), linetype = "dashed", color = "blue") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = x, yend = y_mean), color = "blue", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = y_hat), color = "darkgreen", linewidth = .5, alpha = .5) +
  labs(title = "SST", subtitle = "Distance: Obs to Mean") +
  theme_minimal()

# 3. Plot SSR: Variation Explained by Regression
# Formula: sum((y_hat - y_mean)^2)
p_ssr <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = y_mean), linetype = "dashed", color = "blue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = y_hat), color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_segment(aes(y = y_hat, xend = x, yend = y_mean), color = "darkgreen", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "SSReg", subtitle = "Distance: Fit to Mean") +
  theme_minimal()

# 4. Plot SSE: Unexplained Variation (Residuals)
# Formula: sum((y - y_hat)^2)
p_sse <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(aes(y = y_hat), color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = x, yend = y_hat), color = "red", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "SSE", subtitle = "Distance: Obs to Fit") +
  theme_minimal()

# 5. Combine Plots
(p_sst | p_ssr | p_sse) 
```
 

## But, we work with sum of **squares**

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# 1. Setup minimal data
set.seed(1)
n <- 6
x <- c(1, 2.5, 4, 6, 8, 9.5)
y <- c(1.5, 4, 3.5, 7, 7.5, 10)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

# Fit model
fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = df)
df$y_hat <- predict(fit)
df$y_mean <- mean(df$y)

# Helper function to create squares
# The side of the square is the absolute difference between y1 and y2
make_squares <- function(data, y1_col, y2_col, color) {
  data$diff <- data[[y1_col]] - data[[y2_col]]
  geom_rect(data = data, aes(
    xmin = x, 
    xmax = x + abs(diff), 
    ymin = pmin(data[[y1_col]], data[[y2_col]]), 
    ymax = pmax(data[[y1_col]], data[[y2_col]])
  ), fill = color, alpha = 0.3, color = color)
}

# 2. Plot SST: Total variation from the Mean
p1 <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = y_mean), linetype = "dashed", color = "blue") +
  make_squares(df, "y", "y_mean", "blue") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "SST", subtitle = "Squares of (Obs - Mean)") +
  theme_minimal() + coord_fixed() # coord_fixed ensures squares look like squares

# 3. Plot SSReg: Variation explained by the line
p2 <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = y_mean), linetype = "dashed", color = "blue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = y_hat), color = "darkgreen") +
  make_squares(df, "y_hat", "y_mean", "darkgreen") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(title = "SSReg", subtitle = "Squares of (Fit to Mean)") +
  theme_minimal() + coord_fixed()

# 4. Plot SSE: Residual variation (the 'error')
p3 <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = y_hat), color = "darkgreen") +
  make_squares(df, "y", "y_hat", "red") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "SSE", subtitle = "Squares of (Obs to Fit)") +
  theme_minimal() + coord_fixed()

# Combine
(p1 | p2 | p3) 
```

##

```{r}
(p1 | p2 | p3) 
```

::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
Linear Regression tilt and shifts the line until the total area of the **red squares** are as small as possible ("least squares")
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
$R^2$: proportion of the blue area (SSTotal) that is successfully covered by the green squares (SSRegr)
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
$R^2_{adj} = 1 - \frac{MSE}{MST}$: same idea, but each model is "charged" for the number of $\beta$'s it uses
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
$h_i$: a point becomes more influential as it moves further away from $\bar{x}$ because the corresponding red square grows quadratically
:::


::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}

Overall F test: $F = \frac{MSReg}{MSE}$

  - is the "average" green square significantly larger than the "average" red square?
    
:::

::: {.fragment}
Sequential sum-of-squares F test: $F=\frac{(SSE(reduced)-SSE(full))/(df_{reduced}-df_{full})}{SSE(full)/df_{full}}$

  - are the red squares for a "larger" model significantly smaller than the red squares for a "smaller" model?
    
:::

:::

## 

::: medium

- Linear Regression tilt and shifts the line until the total area of the **red squares** are as small as possible ("least squares")
- $R^2$: proportion of the blue area (SSTotal) that is successfully covered by the green squares (SSRegr) 
- $R^2_{adj} = 1 - \frac{MSE}{MST}$: same idea, but each model is "charged" for the number of $\beta$'s it uses
- $h_i$: a point becomes more influential as it moves further away from $\bar{x}$ because the corresponding red square grows quadratically
- Overall F test: $F = \frac{MSReg}{MSE}$
    - is the "average" green square significantly larger than the "average" red square?
- Sequential sum-of-squares F test: $F=\frac{(SSE(reduced)-SSE(full))/(df_{reduced}-df_{full})}{SSE(full)/df_{full}}$
    - are the red squares for a "larger" model significantly smaller than the red squares for a "smaller" model?

:::

## Today: building an *explanatory* model

:::: {.columns align=center}
::: {.column width="25%"}
**Question:**
:::

::: {.column width="75%"}
How are weekends and holidays associated with ridership, after accounting for the weather?
:::
::::

<br>

. . .

Two reasons to build a model:

- **Explanatory:** understand the relationship between the response and particular predictors. We care about the *coefficients* (today!)
- **Predictive:** make accurate predictions for *new* data. We care about the *predictions* (after the quiz)

## Idea: how do we decide what variables to include? {.smaller}

```{r}
bikes |> head(10) |> knitr::kable()
```

::: {.task .medium}
Which variables would you include to answer our question? Why?
:::

## A recipe for explanatory models

::: {.incremental}
1. **Start with the question.** Which variables are you interested in? Which do you need to adjust for? These stay in the model, even if they aren't "significant"
2. **Look before you fit.** Check for predictors that carry (almost) the same information
3. **Fit a *small* set of candidate models** (not every possible combination!)
4. **Compare the candidates**: $F$ test for nested models; adjusted $R^2$, AIC, or BIC for any models
5. **Check the conditions** for the model you choose
6. **Interpret and justify** your choice
:::

::: notes
Timing: framing + recipe ~5 min. Keep coming back to this slide; each section below is one step.
:::

## Step 1: Our candidate models

- **Interested in:** `weekend`, `holiday`
- **Adjust for:** weather (temperature, windspeed, humidity)

```{r}
tibble(Model = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"),
       Predictors = c("temp_actual + windspeed + weekend",
                      "A + holiday",
                      "B + humidity",
                      "C + temp_feel",
                      "temp_feel + humidity + weekend + holiday")) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## Step 2: Look before you fit

```{r}
#| echo: true
bikes |>
  select(temp_actual, temp_feel, windspeed, humidity) |>
  cor() |>
  round(2)
```

. . .

`temp_actual` and `temp_feel` are almost the same variable &rarr; we'd expect multicollinearity if we include both

::: notes
Timing: Steps 1-3 ~13 min (min 17-30).
:::

## Step 3: Compare nested models with an $F$ test

**Which pairs are nested?** Circle one for each.

| Model 1 | Model 2 | Nested? |
|:--|:--|:--|
| A | B | yes / no |
| B | D | yes / no |
| C | E | yes / no |
| A | C | yes / no |

. . . 

$$F = \frac{(SSE_{reduced} - SSE_{full}) / d}{SSE_{full} / df_{full}}$$

-   Numerator: improvement per $\beta$ added
-   Denominator: average variance/noise in the full model
-   A large $F$ means: the bigger model reduces SSE by much more than we’d expect from noise alone.

## Step 3: Compare nested models with an $F$ test

Adding variables one at a time: 

```{r}
step_tab <- bind_rows(
  tidy(anova(bikes_A, bikes_B)) |> slice(2) |> mutate(step = "A to B: add holiday"),
  tidy(anova(bikes_B, bikes_C)) |> slice(2) |> mutate(step = "B to C: add humidity"),
  tidy(anova(bikes_C, bikes_D)) |> slice(2) |> mutate(step = "C to D: add temp_feel")
) |>
  select(step, df = df, F = statistic, `p-value` = p.value) |>
  mutate(`p-value` = fmt_p(`p-value`))

knitr::kable(step_tab, digits = 2)
```

. . .

::: medium
- `holiday`: we keep it no matter what (it's part of our question), but the data also support it
- `humidity`: big improvement in SSE
- `temp_feel`: not much evidence that it helps once we have `temp_actual`
:::

## Careful: `temp_actual` and `temp_feel`

```{r}
bind_rows(
  tidy(bikes_C) |> filter(term == "temp_actual") |> mutate(model = "C (without temp_feel)"),
  tidy(bikes_D) |> filter(term %in% c("temp_actual", "temp_feel")) |> mutate(model = "D (with temp_feel)")
) |>
  select(model, term, estimate, std.error, p.value) |>
  mutate(p.value = fmt_p(p.value)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

::: medium
Standard error of `temp_actual` goes up by a factor of about `r round(summary(bikes_D)$coef["temp_actual", "Std. Error"] / summary(bikes_C)$coef["temp_actual", "Std. Error"], 1)` (VIF $\approx$ `r round(car::vif(bikes_D)["temp_actual"])`)

&rarr; temperature clearly matters, but in model D *neither* temperature variable looks significant on its own 🫠

&rarr; pick one temperature variable
:::

## When the $F$ test can't help

```{r}
#| echo: true
bikes_C <- lm(rides ~ temp_actual + windspeed + weekend + holiday + humidity, data = bikes)
bikes_E <- lm(rides ~ temp_feel + humidity + weekend + holiday, data = bikes)
```

::: task
Is `bikes_E` nested in `bikes_C`? Could we use `anova(bikes_E, bikes_C)`?
:::

. . .

::: medium
- **Non-nested models**: neither is a special case of the other, so the $F$ test does not apply
- **Many candidate models**: each $F$ test needs a nested pair, and repeated testing is a problem
- We need tools that work for *any* two models fit to the same data
:::

## Adjusted $R^2$

::: medium

$R^2_{adj} = 1 - \dfrac{MSE}{MST} = 1 - \dfrac{SSE/(n-(p+1))}{SST/(n-1)}$

  - $R^2$ always goes up when we add predictors; $R^2_{adj}$ can go down
  - can be used for nested and non-nested models
  - no formal test/rules for "better enough" 

:::
    
```{r}
#| echo: true
summary(bikes_C)$adj.r.squared
summary(bikes_E)$adj.r.squared
```


## Information criteria: AIC and BIC

The following "information criteria" can be used to compare nested or non-nested models (smaller values are better)

$$IC = \text{Measure of Fit} + \text{Penalty}$$

<br>

$$AIC = n \log(SSE/n) + 2(p+1)$$

$$BIC =  n \log(SSE/n) + \log(n) \cdot (p+1)$$

::: medium
$p$ = number of predictors in the model. Fit term gets smaller with a bigger model; the penalty gets bigger. BIC penalizes more than AIC (since $\log(n) > 2$ when $n \ge 8$)

In R: `AIC(model)` and `BIC(model)`
:::

## Example: adjusted $R^2$ and $F$ tests by hand

A researcher fits four nested models to $n = 40$ observations. Fill in the
table, then answer the questions.

| Model | Predictors | $p$ | SSE | $\hat\sigma^2 = SSE/(n-(p+1))$ | $R^2_{adj}$ |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| M0 | none | 0 | 980 | 25.13 | 0 |
| M1 | $x_1$ | 1 | 520 | 13.68 | 0.455 |
| M2 | $x_1, x_2$ | 2 | 410 | | |
| M3 | $x_1, x_2, x_3$ | 3 | 398 | | |

$R^2_{adj} = 1 - \hat\sigma^2 / \hat\sigma^2_{M0}$ (since $MST = SSE_{M0}/(n-1)$).
$F = \frac{(SSE_{reduced} - SSE_{full}) / d}{SSE_{full} / df_{full}}$

## 

**(a)** Which model is best by $R^2_{adj}$?

<br>

**(b)** Use an $F$ test to compare M3 to M2. State $d$ and $df_{full}$. (reminder: $F = \frac{(SSE_{reduced} - SSE_{full}) / d}{SSE_{full} / df_{full}}$)

<br>

**(c)** Do the two tools agree? Which model would you choose?

<br>

## Step 4: Compare all of our candidates

Open up the R activity for today and work through parts 1-3 in your groups

## Step 4: Compare all of our candidates


```{r}
mods <- list("A: temp + wind + weekend" = bikes_A,
             "B: A + holiday" = bikes_B,
             "C: B + humidity" = bikes_C,
             "D: C + temp_feel" = bikes_D,
             "E: temp_feel + humidity + weekend + holiday" = bikes_E)

tibble(Model = names(mods),
       k = map_int(mods, ~length(coef(.x))),
       `Adj R2` = map_dbl(mods, ~summary(.x)$adj.r.squared),
       AIC = map_dbl(mods, AIC),
       BIC = map_dbl(mods, BIC)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = c(0, 0, 3, 1, 1))
```

::: medium
- Model C beats model E under every criterion, which no $F$ test could tell us
- C vs D: adjusted $R^2$ and AIC *slightly* prefer D, BIC prefers C. When the tools disagree (and there's multicollinearity!), choose the simpler model
:::

## Comparing two models

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    classDef default fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px,color:#1b5e20;

    A(["Are the models nested?"])
    B(["Do they differ by<br>one coefficient?"])
    C["t-test for that coefficient<br>(same as the F test)"]
    D["Extra sums of squares F test<br>anova(reduced, full)"]
    E["Adjusted R², AIC, or BIC<br>(no p-value)"]
    F["If the tools disagree,<br>choose the simpler model"]

    A -->|YES| B
    A -->|NO| E
    B -->|YES| C
    B -->|NO| D
    C --> F
    D --> F
    E --> F
```

## Summary

::: medium

| Tool | Nested only? | p-value? | Notes |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| $F$ test | Yes | Yes | The formal test for nested models |
| Adjusted $R^2$ | No | No | Easy, but no rule for "better enough" |
| AIC | No | No | Most willing to add terms |
| BIC | No | No | Most conservative |

:::

- Use domain knowledge first. Tools compare candidate models; they don't replace thinking.
- **Justify your model choice!**

## Appendix: Sequential ANOVA (the `anova()` function) {visibility="hidden"}

::: medium

When you use `anova()` on a single model, R provides a table of **extra Sum of Squares (SS)** for terms added sequentially

```{r}
#| echo: true
model_1 <- lm(rides ~ temp_actual + windspeed + weekend + temp_actual:weekend + 
                windspeed:weekend, data = bikes)
anova(model_1)
```

:::

## Appendix: How do the tools relate? {visibility="hidden"}

For the bikes data ($n = $ `r n_bikes`), adding $d = 1$ parameter, the larger model is preferred when

```{r}
df_f <- bikes_A$df.residual
tibble(Rule = c("F test, $\\alpha = 0.05$", "AIC", "BIC"),
       `Prefers larger model if F is bigger than` = c(qf(0.95, 1, df_f),
                                                      df_f * (exp(2 / n_bikes) - 1),
                                                      df_f * (n_bikes^(1 / n_bikes) - 1))) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

## Appendix: Overfitting (move to prediction day) {visibility="hidden"}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2

set.seed(123)
n <- 30
x <- seq(0, 1, length.out = n)
y <- sin(2 * pi * x) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

plot_fit <- function(degree, title) {
  ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "black") +
    stat_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ poly(x, degree), 
                se = FALSE, color = "#f15a31", linewidth = 1) +
    labs(title = title) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
}

(plot_fit(1, "Underfit") | plot_fit(3, "Balanced") | plot_fit(15, "Overfit"))
```
